claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy can exist in either a random-solid-solution state or an equilibrium state containing chemical short-range order.
The target HfNbTaTiZr-type alloy remains single-phase bcc in the stated high-temperature regime.
Standard interatomic potentials fail to capture SRO evolution in the target alloy.
Thermomechanical processing or annealing can produce and eventually percolate SRO clusters in a single-phase bcc refractory alloy.
An SRO correlation length greater than the phonon mean free path creates a connected SRO network.
The alloy remains single-phase bcc above approximately 1000 K.
Approaching but not exceeding the order-disorder transition temperature preserves SRO without producing a fully ordered precipitate phase.
Percolated SRO clusters form coherent interfaces with the random matrix.
Chemically ordered SRO domains have less lattice distortion than the random matrix.
Reduced lattice distortion in the SRO network lowers its phonon-scattering cross-section.
Isolated SRO clusters scatter phonons and reduce thermal conductivity.
Percolation converts SRO clusters into a continuous low-disorder transport pathway.
The percolated ordered network supports ballistic phonon transport that bypasses scattering centers in the random matrix.
Percolating SRO produces a net increase in thermal conductivity that exceeds serial or parallel mixing-model predictions.
Thermal conductivity undergoes a sharp, non-linear increase at a critical SRO volume fraction or correlation length.
Above the percolation threshold, thermal conductivity becomes significantly greater than the random-solid-solution baseline.
Thermal conductivity in the random solid solution or non-percolating state is dominated by point-defect and mass-fluctuation scattering.
The proposed effect requires SRO percolation without ordered-phase precipitation or grain-boundary segregation.
An inaccurate potential-energy surface can mispredict the energy cost of SRO-network formation and the associated transition temperature.
The hypothesis can be tested by correlating thermal conductivity with independently measured SRO size and connectivity across samples processed to span non-percolating and percolating states.
